Notes · Canvas & Mobile

React and a game loop in the same page

Orbit Defender is a 2D shooter written in React and drawn in a canvas, then packaged for Android. The interesting problems were not in the game — they were in the seam between a framework built around re-rendering and a loop that must run sixty times a second regardless.

The seam is the whole problem

React is designed to re-render when state changes. A game loop changes state constantly and draws every frame. Put the two together naively and you get the worst of both: the canvas redraws on React's schedule instead of the frame's, and every bullet becomes a state update that queues a render you never wanted.

The rule that fixed it: the loop owns the world, React owns the shell. The simulation lives in plain objects updated by a single loop. React renders the parts a person reads — score, lives, the level readout, the buttons — and those update on a slow, deliberate cadence rather than on every frame. Two clocks, each running at the speed it was built for.

Touch controls that do not fight the thumb

A mouse reports a position. A thumb covers the thing it is pressing. Everything that works on desktop — a small target, a hover state, a control in the corner — has to be re-decided for a finger.

  • The fire control sits where the thumb already is, not in a corner the hand has to travel to. In this build it is the large circular button under the right thumb, and it is always in the same place so the player can learn it without looking.
  • Dragging is the movement, not the aiming. The ship follows the finger; the weapon fires where the ship is. One gesture, one meaning.
  • No hover, no ambiguity. Anything that would have been a hover state on desktop becomes a visible, permanent label on touch.

The game state a level actually needs

The temptation is to model the game as a single object that grows. What works better is a small explicit set of states — playing, paused, dead, restarting — with the loop reading the state rather than being told what to do. When the ship dies, the loop does not stop; it keeps running and simply stops spawning, so the death is visible in the world instead of a freeze.

The same discipline applies to weapons. Scatter, laser and plasma are not three code paths through the update loop; they are data — fire rate, spread, damage, projectile speed — read by one path. Adding a fourth weapon is then a row, not a branch.

What packaging changes

Capacitor turns the same page into an Android app. What it changes is less about the code and more about the contract: the app now has a fixed screen, a known GPU, no address bar, and a user who expects it to open instantly and remember where they were.

The canvas benefits most — a phone that runs the page in a browser has to compete with tabs and scrolling; the same phone running it as an app does not. The parts that needed care were the ones the browser used to handle for free: back navigation, the safe area at the top of the screen, and the fact that there is no refresh button to recover from a bad state.

The project

A top-down space shooter for Android — scatter, laser and plasma weapons, bombs, shields and a boss that announces itself. React for the shell, Canvas 2D for the game, Capacitor for the package.
